segments.text: Well, I think that's out of order.
So respectfully, I disagree, Judge.
I think that's out of order.
I'm not saying that's what I'm saying.
I'm saying that's what they're saying.
Yeah, the order is we can do you can do a lot of things under the contract.
And if you're wrong, there's other provisions and other places that tell you you're wrong.
There is a requirement from the opposing party, whether it be the employer or the union, to come forward and say, hey, you're wrong on this.
And you got 30 days to do that.
Otherwise, it's like a statute of limitations and it becomes final.
And that's our position in this case.
So that's where we are.
So, and when we look at the, you know, I wanted to talk about delegation as well.
When you look at the delegation issue, I think that's the clearest issue in this case.

I think where the court errors and it delegates arbitrability decisions on everything to the arbitrators, this is a contract under SEIU which does not have clear and unmistakable evidence of delegation of any of these three issues I've been talking about.
To the arbitrators.
All those gateways.
The stage is more like interstate distributor than SEIU, is it not?
No, I'm just the distinction between interstate distributors is the absence of any arguments of timeliness or the filing of a grievance.
That does not appear in interstate distributors.
So, interstate distributors is purely an interpretation case about a termination clause.
It's not a failure to grieve clause.
Would you agree that if the contract required
You to bring your action, if you will, to terminate before the arbitrators.
And if you didn't do that, you've got a problem, right?
Yes.
And that's essentially what happened here.
They said, hey, wait a minute, you've said you want to terminate this, but you talked to the wrong people.
I think the situation you're expressing would be if on March 27th, the letter sent out that's repudiating the contract.
And anytime within that 30 days they come in and say, hey, you can't do this.
We're going to grieve it and challenge this, then we may have very well had a problem.
But then we were allowed to then take action to either back out of that or to make a decision to fight it on whatever arguments we wanted to fight it.
And it would have been resolved before the contract even ended.
And there would have been no prejudice of anybody moving down the road and using non-union labor.
Their inaction, their inability to abide by a clear cut directive of the contract, reve these things within thirty days, is what has prejudiced us and has harmed my client.
Okay, do you want to save some of this time?
It's entirely up to you, but do you want to rebut
Later on, with the time you've got, yeah, I'm just going to add one 30-second remark and I'll see you in three minutes.
Thank you, Judge.
So, just on the delegation issue, I think it's clear that it has to be reversed just on the delegation issue.
These are all issues the district court judge needed to consider, all the arbitrability issues, even the one you're talking about, repudiation.
And she passes all that on to the arbitrators, and that was error.
So, and the first and foremost, and it's just under the clear-cut standard of SEIU, you need some clear and unmistakable evidence.
That the arbitrators have jurisdiction of arbitrability.
And in the absence of that, the district court has to decide it.
The district court didn't decide that, doesn't even discuss timeliness or the failure to grieve.
Thank you.
Okay, very well.
Let's hear from the union.
This is Mr.
